# TDPdf v1.25.0.0

**TDPdf now notices when a new release exists, and on a managed device asks Intune to come and get it.**

## Why

Yesterday, hours after 1.24.1.0 shipped a fix for text boxes, a machine was found still running 1.23.5.0 — six releases behind. In one 28-minute session its user placed 32 text boxes and got nothing from any of them. Every one of those six releases had fixed the defect they were hitting. None had reached them.

Nothing on that machine was broken. Intune polls on its own schedule, roughly every eight hours and only when the device is awake and checking in, and that machine had simply not been told. The one thing that always knows a device is in use is the application the person is sitting in front of, so that is now what asks.

TDPdf checks twice a day whether a newer release exists. On an enrolled device it responds by running the enrollment client's own sync task — the same thing the Company Portal's **Sync** button does — and Intune comes and fetches the update.

**It never downloads and never installs.** On a managed device the update path is Intune's and stays Intune's: one delivery mechanism, one audit trail, one set of assignments. An application that self-updated underneath Intune would fight the detection rule on every cycle.

The check is an unauthenticated HTTPS request to GitHub's public releases listing. It carries no identifier, no document state, no machine name, and not even the installed version — TDPdf downloads the public version number and compares on the device. It is disclosed to users in `PRIVACY.md`, and an administrator can disable it fleet-wide with `Enabled = 0` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\TDPdf\Update`.

## Installing over a running TDPdf

This is the other half of the same problem, and it had been quietly failing for four releases: the installer crashed with `IOException` whenever the destination was locked, which is exactly what happens when somebody has TDPdf open.

Windows refuses to overwrite an executing file but is perfectly happy to rename one. The installer now displaces the running image and drops the new build into place, so an install succeeds against a machine in active use. The person carries on in the old build until they next start TDPdf — which the status line now tells them, because an update that lands silently is not the same as an update that arrives.

## Also fixed

- **Ctrl+S works while you are typing in a text box** — as do Open, Save As, New, Close, Print, Find and About. All nine were suppressed whenever an annotation text box had focus, so typing an annotation and reaching for Ctrl+S did nothing at all. Nobody could have noticed until now: before 1.24.1.0 the editor was destroyed a few hundred milliseconds after it appeared, so nobody was ever typing in one long enough to reach for a shortcut. Undo deliberately keeps its guard — inside a text box, Ctrl+Z means "undo my typing", and letting the document handler win would silently revert an annotation or a page rotation while you believed you were correcting a word.
- **PDFs whose file name or password contains characters outside the system code page now open.** They were being marshalled through the machine's ANSI code page where PDFium expects UTF-8, so anything the local code page could not represent was corrupted before PDFium saw it, and the document silently failed to load.

## Fork-sync

This release reviewed upstream KillerPDF's `develop/1.8.0` branch and **deliberately did not adopt it**. That branch is unreleased, and its defining change is replacing PdfSharpCore with a bespoke document engine on .NET 10 — nearly every entry in its changelog's *Changed* section reads "now goes through The KillerPDF.Engine". TDPdf's architecture uses three PDF libraries, each for what it is best at, and that swap is ruled out by design; taking it on is a fork-defining decision rather than a sync.

The two fixes credited to upstream above are what the review was worth. Both were upstream's findings, both turned out to be live bugs here, and neither touches their engine. The features that remain genuinely portable are tracked as issues rather than rushed in beside a fleet release.

## What this changes for administrators

**The Intune detection rule now requires 1.25.0.0, so managed machines pick this up on the next evaluation. Assignments are unaffected.** The telemetry configuration is unchanged. One new policy value is available and entirely optional — `Enabled` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\TDPdf\Update` — and four new `Update.*` telemetry events are documented in the administrator guide and `PRIVACY.md`.
